story_type: 1952 atomic test series, warplanes parked near the blasts
hook: In 1952, warplanes were parked in the desert next to atomic bombs.
narration: In nineteen fifty two, warplanes were parked in the Nevada desert, and atomic bombs went off near them.
This was Tumbler-Snapper, a test series run by the Atomic Energy Commission at the Nevada Proving Ground.
The main goal was measuring blast pressure from bombs fired at different heights above the ground.
On one shot, a new kind of pressure wave raced out along the ground ahead of the blast, kicking up a wall of dust.
Fighters and bombers were set out to see what the blast would do to them.
Planes facing the blast head on held up far better than planes hit from the side or the tail.
outcome: The bombers took the blast worse than the fighters, and the films helped set damage rules for aircraft.
title: Warplanes parked next to atomic blasts
description:
In 1952, the Tumbler-Snapper test series at the Nevada Proving Ground measured atomic blast pressures and exposed fighters and bombers to the blasts. This U.S. Air Force Lookout Mountain Laboratory film reports what the tests found.
